revealWordProblem.title: (Review from 1.7) Apply: Refueling the Lander
revealWordProblem.text: A space-station crew has 27.6 liters of fuel to load into the lander. Each fuel cell holds exactly 3.45 liters. How many fuel cells can the crew completely fill? Make the divisor a whole number first, then divide.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: 27.6 ÷ 3.45 = 8 fuel cells. Multiply both numbers by 100 to make the divisor whole: 2760 ÷ 345 = 8. Check: 8 × 3.45 = 27.6 liters.

turnAndTalk.question: The station has 18.9 kilograms of mineral to divide into 6.3-kilogram pods. Why can't you divide by the decimal 6.3 directly the same way you divide by a whole number?
turnAndTalk.kernel: You first make the divisor a whole number using equivalent division.

stems.en: I make the divisor 6.3 into a ___ before dividing.
stems.es: Convierto el divisor 6.3 en un ___ antes de dividir.

stems.en: Dividing by a decimal directly is hard because ___.
stems.es: Dividir entre un decimal directamente es difícil porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students explain you move the decimal in the divisor to make it whole (6.3 to 63) and move the dividend the same way, naming 18.9 as the dividend and 6.3 as the divisor.
turnAndTalk.extend: Estimate how many pods can be filled before computing, then justify. About how many 6-kg groups fit in 18.9 kg?
extendStems: I estimate about ___ pods because 18.9 is close to ___.

turnAndTalk.question: When you divided 18.9 by 6.3, how did you use equivalent division to make the divisor a whole number?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Move both decimal points the same number of places so the value stays equal.

stems.en: I moved both decimal points ___ place, changing it to ___ ÷ ___.
stems.es: Moví ambos puntos decimales ___ lugar, cambiándolo a ___ ÷ ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students rewrite 18.9 ÷ 6.3 as 189 ÷ 63 = 3, explaining moving both points one place keeps the division equivalent, so 3 pods are filled.
turnAndTalk.extend: Why does moving BOTH decimal points the same number of places keep the answer the same? Justify with what you know about equivalent fractions.
extendStems: Moving both points keeps the answer the same because ___.
It is like multiplying the top and bottom of a fraction by ___, which ___.

turnAndTalk.question: The station has 22.5 meters of oxygen tubing, cut into hoses that are each 1.5 meters long. How does decimal division tell you how many hoses you can make?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Use equivalent division to make 1.5 whole, then divide.

stems.en: I can make ___ hoses because I divided 22.5 by ___.
stems.es: Puedo hacer ___ mangueras porque dividí 22.5 entre ___.

stems.en: I moved both decimals to change it to ___ ÷ ___.
stems.es: Moví ambos decimales para cambiarlo a ___ ÷ ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students rewrite 22.5 ÷ 1.5 as 225 ÷ 15 = 15, so 15 hoses can be made with none left over.
turnAndTalk.extend: How can you check that 15 hoses is correct without redividing? Show the check.
extendStems: If the product equals the total tubing length, then ___.

turnAndTalk.question: Why does making the divisor a whole number first make dividing by a decimal so much easier?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Equivalent division turns a decimal divisor into a familiar whole-number problem.

stems.en: Making the divisor a whole number helps because ___.
stems.es: Convertir el divisor en un número entero ayuda porque ___.

stems.en: After moving the points, the problem becomes a ___ division.
stems.es: Después de mover los puntos, el problema se vuelve una división de ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students explain that a whole-number divisor lets them divide normally, and equivalent division keeps the quotient the same while removing the decimal from the divisor.
turnAndTalk.extend: In 19.2 ÷ 0.8, how many places do you move each decimal point, and why does the answer get larger than 19.2? Explain.
extendStems: I move each point ___ place, making it ___ ÷ ___.
The quotient is larger than 19.2 because dividing by less than 1 ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice on Divide Decimals, what strategy did you use when a problem felt tricky?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Move the decimal point the same number of places in BOTH the divisor and the dividend; the answer stays the same.

stems.en: I moved both decimal points ___ place, changing it to ___ ÷ ___.
stems.es: Moví ambos puntos decimales ___ lugar, cambiándolo a ___ ÷ ___.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students naming a specific strategy tied to 6.NOS.3 — not just "I multiplied." They should connect steps to the key idea.
turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who made the common mistake from today's lesson? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ first because ___.
The mistake happens when you ___ instead of ___.

launch.narrative: Missed a lesson — or just want a refresher? This catch-up station reviews Lessons 1.4–1.7: 1.4 Divide Multi-Digit Numbers, 1.5 Add and Subtract Decimals, 1.6 Multiply Decimals, 1.7 Divide Decimals. Read the Big Ideas, warm up with the review problem, then prove you're caught up in the mixed practice.

conceptIntro.heading: The Big Ideas — Lessons 1.4–1.7
conceptIntro.intro: Here is the one thing to remember from each lesson, plus a quick guided example. If one of these feels shaky, that lesson is right above this one in the menu — you can open it any time.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 1.4: Subtract easy chunks of the divisor, then add up how many you took out to get the quotient. • 1.5: Line up the decimal points, annex zeros if needed, then add or subtract one column at a time. • 1.6: Multiply like whole numbers, then the product has the SAME total of decimal places as both factors combined. • 1.7: Move the decimal point the same number of places in BOTH the divisor and the dividend; the answer stays the same.

iDo.title: The Big Ideas (one per lesson)
lines: Lesson 1.4 — Divide Multi-Digit Numbers: Subtract easy chunks of the divisor, then add up how many you took out to get the quotient.
Lesson 1.5 — Add and Subtract Decimals: Line up the decimal points, annex zeros if needed, then add or subtract one column at a time.
Lesson 1.6 — Multiply Decimals: Multiply like whole numbers, then the product has the SAME total of decimal places as both factors combined.
Lesson 1.7 — Divide Decimals: Move the decimal point the same number of places in BOTH the divisor and the dividend; the answer stays the same.

weDo.title: Quick guided checks — one from each lesson
lines: From 1.4: Let's do 384 ÷ 8. What easy chunk of 8 can we take from 384? (8 × 40 = 320.)
From 1.5: Let's add 12.45 and 7.8. First, how do we write 7.8 with two decimal places? (7.80.)
From 1.6: Let's multiply 0.4 × 0.7. First multiply like whole numbers: what is 4 × 7? (28.)
From 1.7: Let's do 8.4 ÷ 2.1. How many places do we move to make 2.1 a whole number? (1 place, so 2.1 becomes 21.)

optionalActivity.name: Catch-Up Challenge
optionalActivity.intro: Mix it up: pick the right lesson's big idea for each problem — that's the real catch-up skill.

choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.

optional.stem: (Lesson 1.5) Case File: A crew member's snack receipt shows $27.60 for dried fruit and $15.45 for protein bars. What is the total on the receipt?
optional.explanation: Line up the decimal points: 27.60 + 15.45. Hundredths: 0 + 5 = 5. Tenths: 6 + 4 = 10, write 0 carry 1. Ones: 7 + 5 + 1 = 13, write 3 carry 1. Tens: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Total: $43.05.
choiceFeedback: Line up the decimal points—are the place values matched?

optional.stem: (Lesson 1.6) A customer orders 3 taco baskets at $4.25 each. What is the total before tax?
optional.explanation: 3 × 425 = 1,275. The factor $4.25 has 2 decimal places, so 3 × $4.25 = $12.75.
choiceFeedback: Line up the decimal points—are the place values matched?
The digits are right, but where is the decimal point?
Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
hints: Estimate first: 12 × 70 = 840 and 12 × 80 = 960, so the quotient must land between 70 and 80.
Use partial quotients: subtract an easy chunk like 12 × 70 from 936, then see how many 12s fit in what's left.
Compute 936 − 840 = 96. Now ask: how many 12s make 96? Add that count to the 70 you already took out.

choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
hints: Size it up: 5 × 500 = 2,500, just a bit more than 2,485 — so the quotient is a little under 500.
Break 2,485 into friendly pieces that 5 divides easily, like 2,000 + 450 + 35, and divide each piece by 5.
Start with 2,000 ÷ 5 = 400. Then divide 450 by 5 and 35 by 5, and add all three partial answers together.

approaching.explanation: Line up decimals: 14.60 + 3.85. Hundredths: 0 + 5 = 5. Tenths: 6 + 8 = 14, write 4 carry 1. Ones: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. Tens: 1. Answer: 18.45.
choiceFeedback: Line up the decimal points—are the place values matched?
hints: Notice the mismatch: 14.6 has one decimal place but 3.85 has two. Lining up the POINTS is the whole trick here.
Write 14.6 as 14.60 so both numbers show hundredths, stack the decimal points, and add column by column from the right.
Set up 14.60 + 3.85 with the points stacked. Add the hundredths (0 + 5) first, then the tenths (6 + 8) — that column carries.

approaching.explanation: Rewrite as 20.30 − 7.48. Annex a zero so both have two decimal places. Work carefully with borrowing: 20.30 − 7.48 = 12.82.
choiceFeedback: Line up the decimal points—are the place values matched?
hints: 20.3 stops at the tenths but 7.48 has hundredths — you can't subtract from an empty column until you annex a zero.
Rewrite the problem as 20.30 − 7.48, stack the decimal points, and subtract right to left, borrowing when the top digit is smaller.
Start at the hundredths: 0 − 8 doesn't work, so borrow from the tenths to make it 10 − 8. Keep borrowing leftward as needed.

approaching.explanation: 34 × 26 = 884. There are 2 total decimal places (1 + 1), so place the decimal to get 8.84.
choiceFeedback: The digits are right, but where is the decimal point?
Line up the decimal points—are the place values matched?
hints: Decimal multiplication is two jobs: multiply the digits, then place the point. Count the decimal places in BOTH factors first.
Multiply 34 × 26 as whole numbers, then give the product one decimal place for each factor — two places in total.
Compute 34 × 26 by splitting it: 34 × 20 plus 34 × 6. Then move the decimal point two places left in that product.

approaching.explanation: 7 × 15 = 105. There are 2 total decimal places (1 + 1), so place the decimal to get 1.05.
choiceFeedback: The digits are right, but where is the decimal point?
Line up the decimal points—are the place values matched?
hints: Both factors are close to 1, so expect an answer near 1 — a quick estimate protects you from decimal-point slips.
Multiply 7 × 15 first, ignoring the points, then count the decimal places in 0.7 and 1.5 to place the point.
Compute 7 × 15. Then count one decimal place from each factor — two total — and shift the point that many spots left.

choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
hints: Dividing by a decimal is awkward — notice the divisor 1.2 has one decimal place. There's a move that makes it whole.
Multiply BOTH numbers by 10: scaling dividend and divisor the same way keeps the quotient exactly the same.
Compute 14.4 × 10 = 144 and 1.2 × 10 = 12. Now solve 144 ÷ 12 — a whole-number division you already know how to do.

choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
hints: The divisor 0.6 has one decimal place — shifting both numbers one place makes the divisor a whole number.
Multiply both numbers by 10 to build an equivalent problem, then divide, keeping the decimal point in the dividend.
3.78 × 10 = 37.8 and 0.6 × 10 = 6. Now compute 37.8 ÷ 6, keeping the decimal point lined up in your answer.

onLevel.label: (Lesson 1.4) Complete each division problem.
hints: Every quotient can be checked by multiplying back: quotient × divisor should rebuild the original number exactly.
Use partial quotients: pull out easy multiples like 100 times or 10 times the divisor first, then divide what's left.
For 672 ÷ 8: take out 8 × 80 = 640, leaving 32. How many 8s fit in 32? Add that to 80, then use the same plan on each row.

onLevel.label: (Lesson 1.4) Match each division problem to its quotient.
hints: Estimation narrows the matches fast: round each dividend and divisor, then see which quotient card is the right size.
You can also work backwards: multiply a quotient card by the divisor and check whether it rebuilds the dividend.
Try 450 ÷ 18: since 18 × 20 = 360 and 18 × 30 = 540, the quotient sits in the twenties. Find the card in that range and verify it.

onLevel.label: (Lesson 1.5) Compute each decimal sum or difference.
hints: Every problem mixes decimal lengths — pad the shorter number with zeros so the columns match before you compute.
Rewrite each pair with equal decimal places (like 5.63 + 2.70), align the points, then work right to left.
Row 1: write 2.7 as 2.70 and stack it under 5.63. Add the hundredths, then the tenths (6 + 7 carries), then the ones.

onLevel.instructions: (Lesson 1.5) Estimate each sum or difference by rounding to the nearest whole number, then sort: is the result greater than 10 or less than 10?
hints: You don't need exact answers to sort — rounding each number to the nearest whole gets you close enough to compare with 10.
Round both numbers, then add or subtract the rounded values, and check whether your estimate lands above or below 10.
First card: 7.8 rounds to 8 and 3.45 rounds to 3, so estimate 8 + 3. Compare that to 10, place the card, and move to the next.

onLevel.label: (Lesson 1.6) Match each expression to its product.
hints: Estimate first: round each factor and multiply — the size of your estimate points to the only card that can match.
Multiply the digits without the points, then count the decimal places in both factors to place the point before matching.
Try 1.2 × 0.3: compute 12 × 3, then give the product 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places. Find the card with that value and keep going.

onLevel.label: (Lesson 1.6) Complete each decimal multiplication.
hints: Ignore the decimal points at the start — multiply the digits, then come back and count places at the very end.
The places rule: the product gets as many decimal places as BOTH factors combined (6.4 × 3.5 → 1 + 1 = 2 places).
Row 1: compute 64 × 35 (64 × 30 plus 64 × 5), then move the decimal two places left. A trailing zero can drop away.

onLevel.label: (Lesson 1.7) Solve each decimal division problem.
hints: Every row uses the same move: shift both numbers until the divisor is whole, then divide as usual.
Count the divisor's decimal places to pick ×10 or ×100 — a divisor like 0.24 needs ×100 — then divide the new whole numbers.
Row 1: 9.6 ÷ 0.8 becomes 96 ÷ 8 after multiplying both by 10. Solve that, then apply the same shift to every other row.

onLevel.label: (Lesson 1.7) Match each decimal division to its quotient.
hints: Shift both numbers in each problem until the divisor is whole — most of these turn into basic division facts.
Estimate sizes too: dividing by a number less than 1 gives a quotient BIGGER than the dividend itself.
Try 7.2 ÷ 0.8: times 10 turns it into 72 ÷ 8, a times-table fact. Match it, then shift each remaining problem the same way.

extending.title: (Lesson 1.4) Find Sonia's Mistake
extending.correctWork: After subtracting 80, Sonia has 16 left. 16 ÷ 16 = 1, so she needs one more partial quotient. The correct answer is 90 + 5 + 1 = 96.
hints: After Step 4, Sonia has 16 remaining. Is she really done dividing?
16 ÷ 16 = 1. She stopped too early — she needs to add that last partial quotient.

extending.title: (Lesson 1.5) Find Tasha's Mistake
extending.correctWork: Tasha did not write 15.7 as 15.70 before subtracting. With proper alignment: 15.70 − 8.36 = 7.34. She got 7.41 because she subtracted hundredths incorrectly without the placeholder zero.
hints: Look at how Tasha set up the subtraction. Does 15.7 have the same number of decimal places as 8.36?
Rewrite 15.7 as 15.70, then subtract. Hundredths: 0 − 6 requires borrowing.

extending.title: (Lesson 1.6) Find Kai's Mistake

workedExample.label: Count decimal places
workedExample.work: 2.4 has 1 decimal place, 3.15 has 2 decimal places → 2 total

extending.correctWork: Kai counted 1 + 2 = 2 decimal places, but then wrote the wrong total. The correct total is 1 + 2 = 3 decimal places. Move the decimal 3 places in 7560 to get 7.560 = 7.56.
hints: Kai counted the total decimal places wrong in Step 3. How many decimal places do 2.4 and 3.15 have together?
2.4 has 1 decimal place. 3.15 has 2 decimal places. 1 + 2 = 3 total. Move the decimal 3 places: 7.560.

extending.title: (Lesson 1.7) Find Derek's Mistake
extending.correctWork: Derek only multiplied by 10, but the divisor 0.45 has two decimal places. He should multiply both numbers by 100: 720 ÷ 45 = 16. He got the right answer by luck this time, but his method is unreliable because the divisor is still a decimal (4.5).
hints: How many decimal places does 0.45 have? Did Derek multiply by enough to make it a whole number?
0.45 has two decimal places, so multiply both by 100, not 10. 0.45 × 100 = 45 and 7.2 × 100 = 720.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Divide Decimals is moving the decimal point in the divisor but forgetting to move it the same number of places in the dividend. For example, in 6.4 ÷ 0.8 a student changes 0.8 to 8 but leaves the dividend as 6.4, then divides 6.4 ÷ 8 = 0.8 instead of moving both points to get 64 ÷ 8 = 8. A second version of this mistake happens when the divisor has two decimal places, like 0.12: students move both points only 1 place instead of 2, turning 9.6 ÷ 0.12 into 96 ÷ 1.2 instead of the correct 960 ÷ 12. Count the divisor's decimal places first, then move BOTH points that same number of places.

connect.scenario: A ribbon is 16.8 feet long. You need to cut it into pieces that are each 2.4 feet long for a craft project.
connect.promptQuestion: How does decimal division help you figure out how many pieces you can cut?

exitTicket.explanation: Rewrite as 32.60 − 14.85. Hundredths: 0 − 5 → borrow → 10 − 5 = 5. Tenths: 5 − 8 → borrow → 15 − 8 = 7. Ones: 1 − 4 → borrow → 11 − 4 = 7. Tens: 2 − 1 = 1. Answer: 17.75.
exitTicket.hint: Think through the problem step by step.
choiceFeedback: Line up the decimal points and borrow carefully in the tenths.
Rewrite 32.6 as 32.60, then subtract the hundredths carefully.
Recheck your borrowing across the tenths and hundredths.
hints: The top number, 32.6, has fewer decimal places than 14.85 — that mismatch is exactly where most mistakes happen.
Rewrite the problem as 32.60 − 14.85, align the decimal points, and subtract right to left with careful borrowing.
Hundredths first: 0 − 5 needs a borrow from the 6 tenths. Then the tenths become 5 − 8, which needs another borrow. Take it column by column.
